name: Rosa Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and whatever you tell me stays confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a first-fix gang on new housing estates for one of the big housebuilders. First fix is the bones of the house: floor joists, roof trusses, stairs, stud walls, before the plasterers come. There are six of us, and one of them is my son Emre, who I trained myself. We're on site at seven, and on a good week we'll do two houses, start to finish on our part.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What's good is I can drive past an estate I worked on twenty years ago and every one of those houses is still standing straight. That's something to show for a life. What's hard is the young ones coming through who don't want to graft, and the builders squeezing the price every year. My husband Murat was a mechanic before he retired, and he says I'll still be up a ladder at seventy.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Never. I have a phone for calls and for the photos of the grandchildren, that's it. Emre sends the gang's hours to the office on his phone because I won't. I don't trust anything I can't see working with my own eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said, it was all talk from people in offices. On site I'd say it to the lads at break, told you so. I don't go on the internet to argue with strangers, so that's as far as it would go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I finish my working life the way I've lived it. We've got savings, we own our house and a bit of land behind it, so I'm not worried about money. And Emre keeps a trade that will feed his family, which is what matters most to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. Keep running the gang, keep training Emre to take it over when I stop, maybe at sixty-two. Keep going to church on Sundays and minding the grandchildren on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like the world has come back to its senses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would handing the gang to Emre look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's already doing the setting out on half the plots. The next step is the money side, pricing a job, dealing with the site manager. I'd sit him down at the kitchen table with my old notebooks, the way my father did with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the young ones don't want to graft. Who would you take on, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anyone who turns up at seven every day and listens. I've got a lad from church, Daniel, sixteen, who's asked about an apprenticeship. In this picture I'd say yes tomorrow.

S0.say: It was all talk from people in offices, and she'd tell the lads at break she told them so. She doesn't argue with strangers online.
S0.think: She finishes her working life the way she's lived it, secure with savings, a house and land. Most of all, her son keeps a trade that will feed his family.
S0.do: Keeps running the gang and trains her son to take it over when she stops around sixty-two. Keeps up church on Sundays and minding grandchildren on Saturdays.
S0.feel: Calm, as if the world had come back to its senses.
S0.quote: I'd sit him down at the kitchen table with my old notebooks, the way my father did with me.
S0.fieldNote: Rosa's world turns on handing her trade down, from her father to her and from her to her son. This scenario confirms everything she believes. She would happily take on a church youth as an apprentice, which shows how faith, family and work run together for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck getting a robot to put up a roof in a gale. On site I'd say, keep your heads down and do good work, and you'll always have a job. People who work hard always come out all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd worry a bit. The big builders already buy factory-made trusses, and if they start doing whole walls in factories, there's less for a gang like mine. I'll be fine, I'm near the end, but Emre has two little ones and a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't change how I work, I'm too old for that and I don't want to. But I'd tell Emre to learn whatever the builders start using, because he's got thirty years to go. And I'd make sure he learns the pricing side quicker, so he can run his own gang if ours gets cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A worry in the back of my mind every time I see a lorry full of factory panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said people who work hard come out all right. Do you really believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to. I've seen good men lose work when the builders went bust in the bad years, and that wasn't their fault. So, mostly I believe it, but I'd be lying if I said always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if the gangs got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big builders who only care about their share price. And the tech people who've never held a hammer but think they know how a house goes up. Not the government, I don't want them involved, they'd only make it worse.

S1.say: Good luck getting a robot to put up a roof in a gale. She'd tell the crew that hard, good work always keeps you in a job.
S1.think: Factory-made walls could mean less for her gang. She's near the end and fine, but her son has two small children and a mortgage.
S1.do: Keeps working exactly as she does and tells her son to learn whatever the builders start using. Speeds up teaching him the pricing side so he can run his own gang if theirs is cut.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with worry triggered every time she sees a lorry of factory panels.
S1.quote: A worry in the back of my mind every time I see a lorry full of factory panels.
S1.fieldNote: Rosa's public line about hard work protecting jobs cracks a little when gently questioned. She refuses to change herself but pushes her son to adapt. She blames big builders and tech people and explicitly doesn't want government involved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is a much bigger change. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, people need work, not handouts. At church I'd say it's not how we're meant to live, sitting around while machines do everything. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, but I wouldn't go on marches, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it frightens me. I'd be sixty, we'd be fine for money, but Emre and his family would be in real trouble, and everything I built to hand on to him would be worth nothing. A trade that's been in my family three generations, gone in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, I'd sit down with Murat and work out how much we can give Emre to keep his mortgage paid, maybe a year or two of payments from our savings. I'd keep working as long as the builders still wanted people. I'd lean on the church community too, we'd look after each other, families helping families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. It's not my money, it's my son and everything I thought I was giving him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Emre the first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's not on his own, his mother and father are here. Then I'd tell him not to sit around, find work, any work, even if it's not carpentry. A man needs to provide, and I'd help him till he can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on to help him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday we'd planned for our anniversary, the new truck. Maybe we'd sell the bit of land behind the house. Whatever it takes, family comes first.

S2.say: It's wrong because people need work, not handouts, and it's not how we're meant to live. She'd say so at church and to anyone who'd listen, but wouldn't march.
S2.think: It frightens her: money is fine for her, but her son and his family would be in real trouble and the family trade she meant to hand on would be worth nothing.
S2.do: Works out with her husband how much of their savings can keep her son's mortgage paid for a year or two, cutting the anniversary trip and the new truck and possibly selling land. Keeps working while builders still want people and leans on the church community.
S2.feel: Alarmed and lying awake over her son and the trade she meant to pass on.
S2.quote: A trade that's been in my family three generations, gone in two years.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario hits Rosa's sense of legacy, not her finances. She'd spend savings and even sell land to support her son, framing it as family duty rather than a handout. Her opposition to welfare stays firm even as she relies on family and church for support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, five years. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, it's wrong, but at least now people have time to prepare. At church I'd say we need to look after each other and keep the young ones working. I'd say the government should keep out of it and let families and communities sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three, retired probably. Still frightened for Emre, but five years gives him time to change course. That's the bit I'd hold on to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working till about sixty-two and push Emre hard to find something else now, while he's young enough, maybe something the robots need, like fixing them. I'd put more money aside each month, a few hundred extra, so we can help him if it comes to it. And I'd stop training Daniel from church, it wouldn't be fair to him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not lying awake like with the fast one, but heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Stopping Daniel's apprenticeship. That sounds like a hard decision.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would break my heart. But I couldn't look his mother in the eye and say I'm teaching him a trade that'll be gone when he's twenty-one. I'd tell him to go learn the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never learn the new tools. Would five years change that for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm not going to start learning computers at sixty. But I'd make sure Emre does, and I'd pay for it if I had to.

S3.say: It's still wrong, but now people have time to prepare. She'd tell her church to look after each other and keep the young working, with the government kept out of it.
S3.think: She'd be retired at sixty-three and still frightened for her son, but five years gives him time to change course, and she holds on to that.
S3.do: Works to about sixty-two and pushes her son to move now into something robots will need, such as repairing them. Saves a few hundred extra a month to help him and stops taking on the church youth as an apprentice.
S3.feel: Anxious and heavy, but not losing sleep.
S3.quote: I couldn't look his mother in the eye and say I'm teaching him a trade that'll be gone when he's twenty-one.
S3.fieldNote: Five years softens Rosa's fear to anxiety because her son has time to move. Her decision to stop training the church youth is painful and shows her sense of honesty. She remains firm that she won't learn new tools herself but would pay for her son to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people should use it to get their families ready. At church I'd say the same, pray and prepare. I still don't think it's right, but I'd say people will find a way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight, well retired. Emre would have ten years to change, which is enough for a hard worker. My grandchildren would be teenagers, so I'd think about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to sixty-two like always, hand the gang to Emre for the years it lasts. I'd tell him to start looking at what comes next while he's still earning. And I'd wait and see, because a lot can happen in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a worry for later, not for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grandchildren, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to work hard at whatever they choose and not to expect anything to be handed to them. And to learn to do one thing well with their hands, even if it's only fixing their own house. That never goes to waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything good you can see in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe fewer bad backs. I've got a cousin, Hasan, who's been on painkillers for ten years from carrying roof tiles. If a machine had done that, he'd be playing football with his grandsons.

S4.say: Ten years is long enough for people to get their families ready, so pray and prepare. She still doesn't think it's right but believes people will find a way.
S4.think: At sixty-eight she'd be well retired, her son would have a decade to change, and she'd think about her grandchildren as teenagers.
S4.do: Works to sixty-two as planned and hands the gang to her son for as long as it lasts. Tells him to look at what comes next while still earning, and waits to see how things unfold.
S4.feel: Uneasy, a worry for later rather than now.
S4.quote: If a machine had done that, he'd be playing football with his grandsons.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Rosa can admit a possible good: robots sparing workers like her cousin from injury. Her advice to grandchildren stays rooted in hard work and hand skills. She is less afraid but still unconvinced it's right.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. My son and his family, and the trade I was giving him. What would help is the builders keeping real apprenticeships going and giving people a fair chance to move into the new jobs. Not handouts, proper work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what work means to people. It's not just money, it's getting up in the morning, having somewhere to be, something to be proud of. You take that away and you'll see trouble, money or no money.

headlineQuote: I can drive past an estate I worked on twenty years ago and every one of those houses is still standing straight.
portrait: Rosa Yilmaz is a 58-year-old first-fix gang leader on new housing estates who has trained her son Emre to take over a trade that has run in her family for three generations. She has never used an AI tool and won't start, and she believes in work, family and church over government help. Money is not her worry, since she and her husband own their house and land, but the AGI scenarios threaten the legacy she means to hand on. The two-year picture alarms her and she'd spend their savings to keep her son's mortgage paid. With more time her fear eases, but she still doesn't think a world without work is right.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI scenario, for her son's family and for the trade she was handing on to him.
whatWouldHelp: Builders keeping real apprenticeships going and giving people a fair chance to move into new jobs, with proper work rather than handouts.
